messages.author: 36dfa8fc10b8b266
messages.subject: Hierarchical model involving complex numbers
parts:
Hello all,

I'm currently working on a model with a custom probability density calculation which involves complex numbers - which, as far as I can tell, is not supported by Stan. I was wondering however if I were to write my own density distribution in C++, would the automatic differentiator be able to handle the complex values, or would it break down?

Thanks for your help,
Dennis

EDIT: Sorry I don't think I made it clear, none of my model parameters need be complex - the complex numbers are just used in calculating the logp__ from my parameters.

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical model involving complex numbers
parts:
Hi Dennis,

You should be able to write your own probability density calculation with complex numbers by representing the real and imaginary parts with two parameters, unless I'm missing something fundamental.

Re: C++, do you have a class that represents a complex number? I don't think there's a straightforward way to go from the Stan language, extend it to a new type, have that type represented in C++ somehow, pass that through functions with different signatures, then get that back out to the interfaces. But... if you wanted to write C++, that's easy. If you also represented complex numbers as 'vector[2]' in the Stan language, that should work as a proof of concept.

If you have a description of this density function, that would help. Either code or latex will do.


Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical model involving complex numbers
parts:
To do that in Stan you'd need to define functions for all the
complex operations and treat the vector as a 2 x N vector with
a real and imaginary component. Then you could write that recursive
equation (you'd need a base case, though!).

I don't know that it'll be easier to do in C++. The point is
that Stan's going to need gradients with respect to all the parameters
and expects a templated functor it can automatically differentiate,
which means something implemented with our library of functions where
the partials are known.

If you define the functions in Stan, this'll all happen automatically,
by the way.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Hierarchical model involving complex numbers
parts:
Hello,

I realise that because I have non-linear transformations of my parameters I need to increment logp by the log Jacobian determinant of the complete inverse transform, but I am really confused about where to start on finding this.

I have a Nx1 vector of resistivities, R, which I transform into a complex value Z (which I am representing as a 1x2 vector). What I think I need to do is to rewrite the transformation and take the derivative of each R[i] w.r.t. Z - using complex differentiation - but that doesn't leave me with a square Jacobian.

If anyone could put me on the right track it would be much appreciated!

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical model involving complex numbers
parts:
There is not going to be any need for complex differentiation — in fact it
will probably be easier to write out your entire model in terms of the
real-valued components (especially if your likelihood depends on only
the magnitude of the complex numbers).

In any case, you cannot map an N-dimensional distribution into
an (M != N)-dimensional one as probability will not be conserved.
What you have to do is engineer an N->N map and then marginalize.
For example,

p(x, y)
-> p( f(x, y), y) | d (f, y) / d (x, y) | (f, y) 
-> \int dy p( f, y) | d (f, y) / d (x, y) | (f, y)

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical model involving complex numbers
parts:
There an infinite number of possible transforms — it’s a bit of
an art finding one that is computationally convenient.  Setting
everything to the same output value and then summing may
not be particularly useful as the Jacobian will be nontrivial and
likely prevent an analytic sum.  The strategy that I’ve most often
seen is one I originally described — fill in the (M - N) missing
entries with the last (M - N) original parameters.
Would you be able to explain how I can find an N->N transformation? Can I do something arbitrary like have each entry equal to 1/N of the end value and sum over them afterwards?
